title: 10.1 Small Group · Group 2
contentObjective: I can find applications of math outside of school — in professions like being a chef, in hobbies like gardening, and around my own house, explain why the method works, and use it on a problem I have not seen before.
languageObjective: I can justify my answer to a skeptic and connect it to a second strategy or representation.

turnAndTalk.question: The chef plans a planter that is 4 feet long and 2 feet wide, filled 1 foot deep with soil. What two different things does the chef calculate about that planter, and why are they different?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Area of the planter is 4 × 2 = 8 square feet (how many plants fit); volume is 4 × 2 × 1 = 8 cubic feet (how much soil to buy).

turnAndTalk.question: Turning off the water while brushing saves 4 gallons per brushing, twice a day, for 365 days — a total of 2,920 gallons a year. How is this the same kind of math as the chef ordering ingredients?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Both use multiplication to project a total amount from a smaller repeated quantity: 4 gallons × 2 brushings × 365 days = 2,920 gallons.

turnAndTalk.question: During practice, when a problem gave you a rate — like gallons saved per day — what strategy helped you scale it up to a year?
turnAndTalk.kernel: A rate like 8 gallons a day scales up by multiplying by the number of days: 8 × 365 = 2,920.

launch.narrative: This is your challenge small group for Lesson 10.1. You can already get the answer — so in here the answer is the starting point. We ask when the method holds, when it breaks, and how you would convince someone who disagrees.

conceptIntro.heading: Push further — Math is an integral part of nearly every profession
conceptIntro.intro: You already can do this. So we go up a level, not up a number: find what is always true, show it a second way, and be ready to defend it with a reason instead of an answer.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: People use math every day in their professions and their hobbies — and it is a good tool for solving problems around your house, too — and you can say why it is true, and where it would stop being true.

iDo.title: Watch me find the math in a chef's day
lines: When chefs plan menus, they determine the number of items on the menu and calculate the price point for each item.
They decide on the portion size of each item and project how much food is needed for each day.
They calculate how much of each ingredient to order — that is counting, measuring, and multiplying, all before a single dish is cooked.

weDo.title: Try it together — then prove it
lines: A planter that is 4 feet long and 2 feet wide has an area of 4 × 2 = 8 square feet — that tells us how many plants fit.
If the soil needs to be 1 foot deep, the volume is 4 × 2 × 1 = 8 cubic feet — that tells us how much soil to buy.
Gardeners also measure seed depth and the distance between seeds. What other garden decisions need math?
Now prove it: say why that move had to work at all — not just that it did.
Sentence frame — convince a skeptic: "My method works because ___ . It would stop working if ___ ."

youDo.title: Now you try — and defend it
lines: Try the problems below on your own. Getting the answer is half the work — be ready to say why your method works, and where it would stop working.
Then pick one problem and show it a second way. If two different methods agree, that agreement is your proof.

interactiveVisual.label: The planter: area, then volume when the soil is deep.

explore.instructions: Go deeper: Both columns are full of math — that is the point. A profession and a hobby, and neither one can run without calculating, measuring, and projecting. After sorting, name one more task for each column. As you work, ask yourself WHY it works.

connect.scenario: Math is an integral part of nearly every profession, and many hobbies include applications of math. You just saw it in a restaurant kitchen and a vegetable garden.
connect.promptQuestion: How is math used in another profession or hobby that matters to you?
connect.prompt: Think of a profession or hobby you care about. To do it well, that person might ___ amounts or prices, ___ distances or portions precisely, and ___ ahead so the work gets done on schedule.

check.stem: A chef is deciding how many portions of a new dish to prepare tonight, based on how many customers are expected. Which math task is this?
choices: Projecting how much food is needed for the day
Setting the price of the dish
Naming the dish on the menu
check.explanation: Deciding how many portions to prepare based on expected customers is projecting food needs — a quantity task. Setting the price is a separate math task (not quantity). Decorating and naming a dish are not math tasks at all.

check.stem: A gardener knows the size of their planter box and wants to know how much soil to buy to fill it. What should the gardener calculate?
choices: The number of leaves per plant
check.explanation: Volume measures 3D capacity, which tells you how much soil fills the box. Area (a 2D measure of the top surface) tells you how many plants fit, not how much soil is needed, and perimeter only measures the boundary length.

check.stem: Leaving the water running while brushing wastes an average of 4 gallons compared to turning the water on only to rinse. If one person brushes twice a day for a year (365 days), how many gallons would they save by turning the water off?
check.explanation: 4 gallons × 2 brushings per day × 365 days = 2,920 gallons. 1,460 comes from forgetting to count both daily brushings, 730 comes from using too small a savings amount per brushing, and 5,840 comes from doubling the whole product instead of just the daily brushings.

connect.modelAnswer: A basketball coach uses math constantly. They calculate shooting percentages to decide who takes the last shot, and they plan practice time by dividing 90 minutes among drills. They even measure and compare stats from game to game to see who is improving.

onLevel.stem: One person saves 8 gallons of water a day by turning the water on only to rinse. How much water does that person save in a year (365 days)?
onLevel.explanation: 8 gallons a day × 365 days = 2,920 gallons in a year.
choiceFeedback: 373 comes from adding 8 + 365 instead of multiplying.
1,460 multiplies 365 by 4 — the savings from one brushing — instead of the full 8 gallons a day.
365 is just the number of days; it forgets to multiply by the gallons saved each day.
hints: You know the savings per day.
How many days are in a year?
Multiply 8 × 365.
onLevel.stemEs: Una persona ahorra 8 galones de agua al día al abrir la llave solo para enjuagar. ¿Cuánta agua ahorra esa persona en un año (365 días)?
onLevel.explanationEs: 8 galones al día × 365 días = 2,920 galones en un año.
hintsEs: Conoces el ahorro por día.
¿Cuántos días tiene un año?
Multiplica 8 × 365.

onLevel.stem: If each person in a house saves 2,920 gallons a year, how much does a household of 3 people save in a year?
onLevel.explanation: 2,920 gallons per person × 3 people = 8,760 gallons a year.
choiceFeedback: 2,923 comes from adding 2,920 + 3 instead of multiplying.
973 (about 2,920 ÷ 3) divides instead of multiplying — more people save MORE water, not less.
5,840 multiplies by 2 people instead of 3.
hints: Each person saves the same amount.
3 people, each saving 2,920 gallons.
Multiply 2,920 × 3.
onLevel.stemEs: Si cada persona de una casa ahorra 2,920 galones al año, ¿cuánto ahorra en un año un hogar de 3 personas?
onLevel.explanationEs: 2,920 galones por persona × 3 personas = 8,760 galones al año.
hintsEs: Cada persona ahorra la misma cantidad.
3 personas, cada una ahorrando 2,920 galones.
Multiplica 2,920 × 3.

onLevel.stem: A household of 5 saves 2,920 gallons per person per year. A household of 4 does the same. How much MORE does the household of 5 save than the household of 4?
onLevel.explanation: 5 people save 5 × 2,920 = 14,600 gallons and 4 people save 4 × 2,920 = 11,680 gallons. The difference is 14,600 − 11,680 = 2,920 gallons — exactly one more person's savings.
choiceFeedback: 14,600 is the TOTAL for the household of 5, not the difference between the two households.
11,680 is the TOTAL for the household of 4, not the difference between the two households.
1 is just the difference in the number of people — each of those people saves 2,920 gallons.
hints: How many more people does the bigger household have?
One more person means one more person's yearly savings.
Each person saves 2,920 gallons a year.
onLevel.stemEs: Un hogar de 5 personas ahorra 2,920 galones por persona al año. Un hogar de 4 hace lo mismo. ¿Cuánto MÁS ahorra el hogar de 5 que el de 4?
onLevel.explanationEs: 5 personas ahorran 5 × 2,920 = 14,600 galones y 4 personas ahorran 4 × 2,920 = 11,680 galones. La diferencia es 14,600 − 11,680 = 2,920 galones — exactamente el ahorro de una persona más.
hintsEs: ¿Cuántas personas más tiene el hogar más grande?
Una persona más significa el ahorro anual de una persona más.
Cada persona ahorra 2,920 galones al año.

onLevel.stem: Choose another person who works in a restaurant — not the chef — and describe the math they would use.
onLevel.modelAnswer: A server uses math all shift. They add up each table's bill, calculate the change for customers paying cash, and figure out their tips as a percent of each check. At the end of the night they total their tips to see what they earned.
sentenceStems: A ___ in a restaurant uses math when ___ .
onLevel.stemEs: Escoge otra persona que trabaje en un restaurante — que no sea el chef — y describe las matemáticas que usaría.
sentenceStemsEs: Un(a) ___ en un restaurante usa matemáticas cuando ___ .

extending.label: Each person who rinses instead of running water saves 8 gallons a day. Complete the table.
extending.labelEs: Cada persona que enjuaga en vez de dejar correr el agua ahorra 8 galones al día. Completa la tabla.
hints: Each person contributes the same 8 gallons — equal groups multiply.
To stretch any row to a year, you would multiply by 365 — that is how the 2,920 in this lesson was built.
hintsEs: Cada persona aporta los mismos 8 galones: los grupos iguales se multiplican.
Para extender cualquier fila a un año, multiplicarías por 365: así se construyó el 2,920 de esta lección.
extending.explanation: The savings scale with the household: 3 people save 24 gallons a day, 5 save 40, and 8 save 64. Multiply any row by 365 days and you get the yearly figures the lesson compares — 8 × 365 = 2,920 gallons per person per year.
extending.explanationEs: El ahorro escala con el hogar: 3 personas ahorran 24 galones al día, 5 ahorran 40 y 8 ahorran 64. Multiplica cualquier fila por 365 días y obtienes las cifras anuales que la lección compara: 8 × 365 = 2,920 galones por persona al año.

extending.label: Match each person to the math their real-world task uses.
extending.labelEs: Empareja a cada persona con las matemáticas que usa su tarea del mundo real.

pairs.termEs: Jardinero que llena un cantero de 4 × 2 × 1 pies
Familia que registra su ahorro de agua

hints: Name the quantity each person needs first — amount of ingredients, soil, water, or dollars per unit.
Scaling uses multiplication; comparing uses a rate.
hintsEs: Nombra primero la cantidad que cada persona necesita: ingredientes, tierra, agua o dólares por unidad.
Escalar usa multiplicación; comparar usa una tasa.
extending.explanation: Each career or chore hides a specific tool: the chef scales by a factor, the gardener computes a volume, the family multiplies a daily rate across a year, and the shopper divides to get a unit rate. 'Math is everywhere' is not a slogan — it is that every one of these decisions is a computation.
extending.explanationEs: Cada oficio o tarea esconde una herramienta específica: el chef escala por un factor, el jardinero calcula un volumen, la familia multiplica una tasa diaria por un año y el comprador divide para obtener una tasa unitaria. 'Las matemáticas están en todas partes' no es un eslogan: cada una de estas decisiones es un cálculo.

extending.stem: A gardener's planter has an area of 8 square feet, and each plant needs 2 square feet of space to grow. How many plants fit in the planter?
extending.explanation: 8 square feet ÷ 2 square feet per plant = 4 plants.
choiceFeedback: 16 multiplies 8 × 2 instead of dividing — that would need a much bigger planter.
10 comes from adding 8 + 2 instead of dividing.
6 comes from subtracting 8 − 2 instead of dividing.
hints: You are splitting the area into equal shares of space.
How many groups of 2 square feet fit inside 8 square feet?
Divide 8 by 2.
extending.stemEs: La jardinera de un jardinero tiene un área de 8 pies cuadrados, y cada planta necesita 2 pies cuadrados de espacio para crecer. ¿Cuántas plantas caben en la jardinera?
extending.explanationEs: 8 pies cuadrados ÷ 2 pies cuadrados por planta = 4 plantas.
hintsEs: Estás repartiendo el área en partes iguales de espacio.
¿Cuántos grupos de 2 pies cuadrados caben en 8 pies cuadrados?
Divide 8 entre 2.

extending.stem: What factors do you consider to determine the number of plants you can put in a planter garden? Is the TYPE of plant a factor? Explain your thinking.
extending.modelAnswer: I would consider the area of the planter and how much space each plant needs between it and its neighbors. The type of plant is definitely a factor, because a tomato plant needs much more space than a radish — so the same 8-square-foot planter could hold many radishes but only a few tomato plants.
sentenceStems: The type of plant matters because ___ .
extending.stemEs: ¿Qué factores consideras para determinar cuántas plantas puedes poner en una jardinera? ¿El TIPO de planta es un factor? Explica tu razonamiento.
sentenceStemsEs: El tipo de planta importa porque ___ .

extending.stem: Which statement matches this lesson's big idea?
choices: Math is everywhere — in professions, hobbies, and problems around your house
Math is just a school subject with little relevance outside the classroom
Only professions like chef use math; hobbies do not
Math is only useful for people who work with money
extending.explanation: The summary says it directly. Some people think math is just a school subject. But math is everywhere — in professions, in hobbies, and around the house.
choiceFeedback: That is exactly the belief the lesson set out to disprove.
The gardening half of the lesson showed a HOBBY full of area, volume, and measurement.
The chef, the gardener, and the water problem all used math about food, space, and water — not just money.
hints: Think about all three contexts in this lesson.
A profession, a hobby, and a bathroom sink.
What did they have in common?
extending.stemEs: ¿Cuál enunciado coincide con la gran idea de esta lección?
extending.explanationEs: El resumen lo dice directamente. Algunas personas creen que las matemáticas son solo una materia escolar. Pero las matemáticas están en todas partes — en las profesiones, los pasatiempos y la casa.
hintsEs: Piensa en los tres contextos de esta lección.
Una profesión, un pasatiempo y el lavabo del baño.
¿Qué tenían en común?
choicesEs: Las matemáticas están en todas partes — en las profesiones, los pasatiempos y los problemas de tu casa
Las matemáticas son solo una materia escolar con poca importancia fuera del salón
Solo profesiones como la de chef usan matemáticas; los pasatiempos no
Las matemáticas solo son útiles para las personas que trabajan con dinero

extending.stem: Each person saves 2,920 gallons a year. Which correctly compares households of 3, 4, 5, and 8 people?
extending.explanation: Multiply 2,920 by each household size. For 3 people: 3 × 2,920 = 8,760. For 4 and 5 people: 11,680 and 14,600. For 8 people: 8 × 2,920 = 23,360.
choiceFeedback: 20,440 is 7 × 2,920 — the last household has 8 people, not 7.
Those add the household size to 2,920 instead of multiplying by it.
46,720 is 16 × 2,920 — that doubles the 8-person household instead of computing it.
hints: Each household total is people × 2,920.
Check the last value most carefully.
extending.stemEs: Cada persona ahorra 2,920 galones al año. ¿Cuál compara correctamente hogares de 3, 4, 5 y 8 personas?
extending.explanationEs: Multiplica 2,920 por cada tamaño de hogar. Para 3 personas: 3 × 2,920 = 8,760. Para 4 y 5 personas: 11,680 y 14,600. Para 8 personas: 8 × 2,920 = 23,360.
hintsEs: El total de cada hogar es personas × 2,920.
Revisa el último valor con más cuidado.

extending.stem: Someone says, 'Math is just a school subject. I'll never use it after class.' Using the chef, the gardener, or the water problem, write what you would say back.
extending.modelAnswer: I would say that a chef never stops using math — they calculate prices, portion sizes, and how much of each ingredient to order every single day. Even at home, math showed us that one person who turns off the tap while brushing saves 2,920 gallons a year. You do not escape math after class; you just stop noticing you are using it.
extending.stemEs: Alguien dice: 'Las matemáticas son solo una materia escolar. Nunca las usaré fuera de clase.' Usando al chef, al jardinero o el problema del agua, escribe qué le responderías.

extending.stem: A chef expects 120 customers tonight and projects that 1 out of every 4 will order the soup. Each serving of soup uses 2 cups of broth. How much broth should the chef prepare?
extending.explanation: 120 ÷ 4 = 30 soup orders, and 30 orders × 2 cups each = 60 cups of broth.
choiceFeedback: 240 uses all 120 customers × 2 cups — but only 1 in 4 customers orders the soup.
30 is the number of soup ORDERS; it forgets to multiply by the 2 cups each serving needs.
15 divides the 30 orders by 2 instead of multiplying by 2.
hints: First find how many customers will order soup.
120 ÷ 4 = 30 orders.
Now, how many cups do 30 servings need?
extending.stemEs: Un chef espera 120 clientes esta noche y calcula que 1 de cada 4 pedirá la sopa. Cada porción de sopa usa 2 tazas de caldo. ¿Cuánto caldo debe preparar el chef?
extending.explanationEs: 120 ÷ 4 = 30 órdenes de sopa, y 30 órdenes × 2 tazas cada una = 60 tazas de caldo.
hintsEs: Halla primero cuántos clientes pedirán sopa.
120 ÷ 4 = 30 órdenes.
Ahora, ¿cuántas tazas necesitan 30 porciones?

questions.explanation: 36 × 25 = 900. There are two decimal places in the factors, so the product is 9.00.
4 × 7 = 28. Two decimal places in the factors means the product is 0.28.

questions.stem: A notebook costs $2.45. How much do 6 notebooks cost?
questions.explanation: 245 × 6 = 1,470. With two decimal places, that is $14.70.

questions.stem: In 1.2 × 0.35, how many decimal places does the product have?
questions.explanation: 1 decimal place plus 2 decimal places gives 3. The product is 0.420.
